questions.question_text: Why are case reports and case series considered the simplest forms of descriptive research?

options.text: They require fewer statistical calculations
They examine only a small number of subjects without comparative groups
They do not require informed consent
They cannot identify new diseases
They are always prospective in design

correct_answer.text: They examine only a small number of subjects without comparative groups

questions.explanation: Case reports and series describe characteristics in one or more subjects without comparison to other groups, making them structurally the simplest descriptive design. Options A, C, and E are either incorrect or secondary features. Option D contradicts historical fact (case reports have identified new diseases).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a descriptive observational study?

options.text: Randomised controlled trial
Case-control study
Case report or series
Cohort study
Meta-analysis

correct_answer.text: Case report or series

questions.explanation: Descriptive observational studies are defined as having no control group and being suitable for hypothesis generation rather than testing, with examples explicitly listed as case reports & series, clinical audit, surveys, qualitative studies. Case-control and cohort are analytical observational studies (with controls). RCT is experimental. Meta-analysis is secondary research.

questions.question_text: A census differs from most cross-sectional surveys in which fundamental way?

options.text: It measures different variables than typical surveys
Its sample includes the entire population rather than a subset
It requires prospective data collection methods
It cannot be used to estimate prevalence
It investigates causal associations between variables

correct_answer.text: Its sample includes the entire population rather than a subset

questions.explanation: A census is explicitly described as a special cross-sectional study where the sample includes the whole population instead of a subset. All other characteristics of cross-sectional studies (A, D, E) remain identical. Option C is incorrect because both census and surveys are cross-sectional (static), not prospective.

questions.question_text: A researcher follows a cohort of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis for 5 years, measuring neurobiological markers, psychosocial factors, and subsequent conversion to psychotic disorder. This design would allow direct measurement of which epidemiological parameter?

options.text: Prevalence of psychotic disorders
Incidence of psychotic disorder in the at-risk population
Relative prevalence across ethnic groups
Cross-sectional relationship between markers and psychosis
Odds of conversion given marker status

correct_answer.text: Incidence of psychotic disorder in the at-risk population

questions.explanation: Prospective cohort studies follow subjects from a specified exposure or state forward to detect new cases of outcome, allowing direct measurement of incidence (new cases occurring over time). Prevalence is measured in cross-sectional designs; odds ratios come from case-control studies; relative prevalence is measured cross-sectionally.

questions.question_text: Which statement about uncontrolled trials is most accurate regarding their position in the research hierarchy?

options.text: They provide stronger evidence than randomized controlled trials
They lack a comparison group, limiting causal inference
They are equivalent to ecological studies in design
They directly measure population-level effectiveness
They eliminate selection and recall bias

correct_answer.text: They lack a comparison group, limiting causal inference

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled trials lack comparison groups, preventing valid assessment of intervention effects independent of other factors (confounding, placebo effect, natural recovery). This fundamental design limitation is explicit in the source distinction between experimental types. Options A, C, and D are factually incorrect. Option E overstates bias reduction.

questions.question_text: What is the temporal relationship between exposure and disease in retrospective research designs?

options.text: Exposure occurs before outcome, which is then observed
Both exposure and outcome have occurred before the study begins
Outcome is experimentally induced after exposure measurement
Exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously
The temporal sequence cannot be determined

correct_answer.text: Both exposure and outcome have occurred before the study begins

questions.explanation: Retrospective research as occurring when a group of individuals has been assembled because they have already experienced the exposure in question and outcomes have already occurred. This distinguishes retrospective from prospective designs where outcomes are observed after exposure. Option D describes cross-sectional studies.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study, why cannot incidence be directly calculated even with large sample sizes?

options.text: Cases and controls are selected based on outcome status, not population exposure
The comparison group is always biased
Recall bias prevents accurate exposure estimation
Matching procedures create missing data
Statistical methods for incidence calculation are not applicable

correct_answer.text: Cases and controls are selected based on outcome status, not population exposure

questions.explanation: Case-control studies begin with cases and controls (outcome-based selection) rather than following exposed populations forward in time, so the denominator needed for incidence calculation cannot be determined. The study design structure, not data quality (C) or matching issues (D), prevents this calculation. Options B and E are imprecise.

questions.question_text: A psychiatric researcher is designing a study to identify risk factors for depression in a community sample. Which study design would be most efficient in detecting multiple risk factors and associations?

options.text: Case report
RCT
Cross-sectional survey
Case-control study
Qualitative interviews

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional survey

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional surveys are often cheap and relatively easy to carry out, identifying patterns of disease prevalence and associations. They can assess multiple exposures and outcomes efficiently. For identifying risk factors (aetiology), case-control or cohort studies are better, but cross-sectional studies are reasonable for initial screening of associations in a community sample.

questions.question_text: Which characteristic distinguishes experimental studies from observational cohort studies?

options.text: Experimental studies measure exposure prospectively
Experimental studies involve deliberate manipulation of intervention
Experimental studies follow participants over prolonged time periods
Experimental studies cannot assess incidence rates
Experimental studies begin with diseased subjects

correct_answer.text: Experimental studies involve deliberate manipulation of intervention

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that deliberate manipulation of exposure (intervention) distinguishes experimental from cohort studies. Both may be prospective (A) and follow participants longitudinally (C). Options D and E describe different design features but are not distinguishing characteristics.

questions.question_text: A prospective cohort study follows 10,000 smokers and 10,000 nonsmokers for 20 years, recording lung cancer incidence. Which specific advantage does this design offer compared to a case-control study of the same question?

options.text: It requires less time and expense
It directly measures and compares incidence rates between groups
It eliminates the possibility of recall bias
It can investigate multiple etiological factors simultaneously
It provides better estimates of disease prevalence

correct_answer.text: It directly measures and compares incidence rates between groups

questions.explanation: Cohort studies measure incidence directly by following at-risk populations forward and observing disease development, allowing direct calculation of relative risk and comparison of incidence between exposed and unexposed groups. Case-control studies cannot measure incidence (A is false). Options C, D describe general advantages but B is the specific temporal advantage. Option E describes cross-sectional studies.

questions.question_text: A study reports that alcohol consumption and psychiatric hospitalisations are associated at the population level. Which problem with ecological studies does this finding illustrate?

options.text: Loss to follow-up
Volunteer bias
Ecological fallacy—population-level associations may not reflect individual-level relationships
Selection bias
Recall bias

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy—population-level associations may not reflect individual-level relationships

questions.explanation: Ecological fallacy is the specific limitation where estimates of effect at the ecological (population) level do not equate to estimates at the biological (individual) level. A population-level association between alcohol consumption and hospitalisation does not prove that individuals who drink alcohol are at higher risk—it could reflect other group-level confounders.

questions.question_text: Which statement best explains why case-control studies are considered suitable for investigating diseases of low incidence?

options.text: They measure relative risk accurately
Cases are identified first, eliminating the need to follow large populations forward
They allow for prospective outcome assessment
They require smaller control groups
They eliminate recall bias entirely

correct_answer.text: Cases are identified first, eliminating the need to follow large populations forward

questions.explanation: Case-control studies assemble cases who have already experienced the outcome, thus avoiding the need to follow large populations over time to identify incident cases. For rare diseases, this is highly efficient. Prospective cohort studies of rare outcomes would require prohibitively large sample sizes to identify sufficient cases.

questions.question_text: A researcher examines whether implementation of a new psychosis early intervention program in one region reduces hospitalizations compared to regions without the program. Which bias is this ecological-level design most vulnerable to?

options.text: Recall bias
Selection bias
Ecological fallacy in attributing regional outcomes to individual intervention exposure
Attrition bias
Performance bias

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy in attributing regional outcomes to individual intervention exposure

questions.explanation: Ecological studies examining group-level outcomes (regional hospitalization rates) are vulnerable to ecological fallacy when individual-level conclusions are drawn. Individuals in the intervention region may have different exposure to the program, baseline risk, or other characteristics not captured by regional aggregation.

questions.question_text: Which type of observational study is most suitable for investigating the aetiology of major depression in individuals with a history of trauma?

options.text: Cross-sectional study
Case report
Cohort study
Qualitative study
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Cohort study

questions.explanation: For aetiology questions, cohort studies are ideal because they follow exposed (trauma) and unexposed groups forward in time to assess the development of the outcome (depression), establishing temporal relationships. Case-control studies are also suitable but less ideal than cohort. Cross-sectional studies cannot establish causality for aetiology. ---

questions.question_text: In designing a diagnostic accuracy study for a new screening tool for early psychosis, which comparison is methodologically essential?

options.text: Comparison between treated and untreated patients
Comparison to a gold standard diagnostic method using cross-sectional design
Comparison between multiple screening tools in a case-control format
Longitudinal comparison of screened versus unscreened populations
Ecological comparison across different geographic regions

correct_answer.text: Comparison to a gold standard diagnostic method using cross-sectional design

questions.explanation: Diagnostic assessment of a new tool requires cross-sectional comparison to a gold standard to determine sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. This design allows simultaneous measurement of the new tool and gold standard in the same sample, without requiring prospective follow-up or group comparisons. ---

questions.question_text: An ecological study examining the relationship between regional antipsychotic prescription rates and schizophrenia prevalence finds a strong correlation. Which critical limitation applies to interpreting this finding?

options.text: Lack of statistical power
Ecological fallacy—population-level associations do not equate to individual-level effects
Selection bias
Inability to establish temporal relationships
Problems with internal validity

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy—population-level associations do not equate to individual-level effects

questions.explanation: Ecological fallacy is the key limitation of ecological studies—estimates of effect at the population level do not equate to biological effects at the individual level. A population-level correlation does not imply the same relationship exists within individuals. This is a fundamental methodological limitation unique to ecological studies. ---

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of medication side effects and treatment discontinuation in schizophrenia, which control selection strategy would be most appropriate?

options.text: Hospital patients with schizophrenia who did not discontinue medication
Hospital patients with a different psychiatric disorder
Neighbourhood controls with no psychiatric history
Relatives of patients with schizophrenia
Any available psychiatric patients in the hospital

correct_answer.text: Hospital patients with schizophrenia who did not discontinue medication

questions.explanation: The most appropriate controls are individuals who are identical to cases except for the presence or absence of the outcome (treatment discontinuation). Hospital patients with schizophrenia who continued treatment best match cases (schizophrenia patients with discontinuation) on exposure characteristics, differing only in the outcome of interest.

questions.question_text: A study comparing antipsychotic medication adherence in first-episode psychosis patients measured at baseline and again at 12-month follow-up represents which study design?

options.text: Case report
Cross-sectional study
Prospective longitudinal study
Ecological study
Case-control study

correct_answer.text: Prospective longitudinal study

questions.explanation: Repeated observations in the same population over a prolonged period (baseline and 12-month follow-up) defines a prospective longitudinal study. This design allows measurement of changes in adherence over time and assessment of factors predicting adherence changes. A single cross-sectional measurement would capture adherence at one time point only.

questions.question_text: Which study design is least susceptible to loss-to-follow-up bias?

options.text: RCT
Cohort study
Case-control study
Cross-sectional study
Longitudinal qualitative study

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional study

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that cross-sectional studies have no problems with loss to follow-up or recall bias because they measure exposure and outcome at a single time point. Cohort studies are prospective and experience loss-to-follow-up; case-control studies are retrospective and have recall bias; RCTs and longitudinal studies involve follow-up periods.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines an analytical observational study?

options.text: Description of a single patient's clinical presentation
Comparison of two subject groups with and without a disorder or exposure
Random assignment of subjects to experimental conditions
Collection of qualitative data on patient experiences
Measurement of disease prevalence in a population

correct_answer.text: Comparison of two subject groups with and without a disorder or exposure

questions.explanation: Analytical observational studies compare two groups—one with the disorder/exposure (cases or exposed cohort) and one without (controls). This comparison allows hypothesis testing through observation without experimental manipulation. Case-control and cohort studies are examples. Descriptive studies lack control groups. ---

questions.question_text: In an ecological study examining the association between alcohol consumption per capita and cirrhosis mortality rates across 50 countries, which assumption is made?

options.text: All individuals in each country are equally exposed to the alcohol consumption level
Individual-level data would produce identical associations
Temporal causality flows from alcohol consumption to cirrhosis
Confounding variables are equally distributed across countries
The study is prospective in design

correct_answer.text: All individuals in each country are equally exposed to the alcohol consumption level

questions.explanation: Ecological studies assume all members of a given population are equally exposed and carry the same risk of a disease, disregarding within-group differences. This is a critical assumption that can lead to ecological fallacy. Option B directly contradicts the source's warning about ecological fallacy. Options C, D, and E are not defining assumptions of ecological studies.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study examining the association between childhood abuse and adult personality disorders, temporality is difficult to establish because:

options.text: The study design is prospective
Both exposure and outcome have occurred before data collection begins
Controls cannot be identified
Multiple etiological factors are examined
The outcome is too common

correct_answer.text: Both exposure and outcome have occurred before data collection begins

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are retrospective designs where both exposure and disease have occurred before the onset of the study. This temporal ambiguity makes it difficult to establish whether the exposure preceded the outcome, a key requirement for establishing causality. In contrast, prospective designs have clear temporal precedence.

questions.question_text: A researcher suspects that maternal infection in the first trimester may cause neurodevelopmental disorders in offspring. Which study design would best evaluate this hypothesis?

options.text: Case-control study starting with children diagnosed with neurodevelopmental disorders
Cohort study following pregnant women from first trimester onwards
Cross-sectional study surveying mothers of affected children
Ecological study comparing birth defect rates across countries
Case report of a single affected child

correct_answer.text: Cohort study following pregnant women from first trimester onwards

questions.explanation: This hypothesis requires establishing temporality (infection before neurodevelopmental diagnosis), which only prospective designs accomplish. A cohort study beginning in the first trimester captures exposure before outcome development. Case-control studies work retrospectively, making temporal sequence ambiguous. Cross-sectional, ecological, and case report designs cannot establish causality.

questions.question_text: A clinician conducting a systematic review examines multiple RCTs of cognitive-behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders to determine treatment effectiveness in real-world clinical practice. This represents which type of study methodology?

options.text: Experimental RCT
Pragmatic RCT synthesis
Ecological study
Cohort study
Case-control study

correct_answer.text: Pragmatic RCT synthesis

questions.explanation: Systematic reviews synthesizing pragmatic RCTs are the optimal design to answer questions about treatment effectiveness (real-world applicability). Experimental RCTs address efficacy under controlled conditions, while pragmatic RCTs and their systematic reviews address effectiveness in clinical practice settings.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of oral contraceptive use and myocardial infarction, the researcher recruits cases from hospital cardiac units and controls from the general population. What type of bias is introduced?

options.text: Recall bias
Selection bias in control group definition
Overmatching
Confounding by smoking status
Temporal bias

correct_answer.text: Selection bias in control group definition

questions.explanation: Mixing hospitalized cases with general population controls creates selection bias because the control group is not representative of the same source population as cases. Evidence emphasizes that controls by definition must be identical to cases except for the presence or absence of disease and recruited independently of exposure status. Option A involves exposure recall. Option C relates to matching variables.

questions.question_text: A prevalence study measuring depression rates in a primary care clinic at a single time point is best classified as which study design?

options.text: Case series
Cohort study
Cross-sectional study
Case-control study
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional study

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at a single point in time and directly measure prevalence. Evidence shows these studies describe various attributes of the subjects in a study group but at a single point in time (a snapshot) and are called prevalence studies. Option A describes small series without comparison. Options B and D are analytical and temporal.

questions.question_text: How does matching in case-control studies affect the relationship between cases and controls?

options.text: It makes cases and controls identical in all respects
It ensures exposed and unexposed groups are equally represented
It aligns selected variables (like age and sex) while preserving exposure differences
It eliminates the need for statistical adjustment in analysis
It prevents any selection bias from occurring

correct_answer.text: It aligns selected variables (like age and sex) while preserving exposure differences

questions.explanation: Matching aligns specific variables between cases and controls such as age, sex, etc. to increase comparability while still allowing exposure differences to exist and be measured. It does not make them identical (A), ensure equal exposure distribution (B), eliminate need for adjustment (D), or prevent all bias (E).

questions.question_text: In an experimental RCT of cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders, participants are randomized to CBT or waitlist control. Which aspect distinguishes this from a prospective cohort study of CBT exposure and outcomes?

options.text: The experimental study involves randomization and intervention assignment
The cohort study would be prospective while the RCT is retrospective
The experimental study measures outcomes while the cohort study does not
The cohort study includes more participants
The experimental study eliminates all confounding bias

correct_answer.text: The experimental study involves randomization and intervention assignment

questions.explanation: Experimental design involves deliberate, randomized intervention assignment, whereas cohort studies observe natural exposure patterns. Randomization distinguishes experiments fundamentally. Option B is false (both prospective). Option E is overstated. Options C and D describe study characteristics rather than design differences.

questions.question_text: In a matched case-control study examining pesticide exposure and Parkinson's disease, matching is performed on age and occupational exposure history. Which consequence could result from matching on occupational exposure history?

options.text: Increased statistical power of the study
Inadvertent matching for a putative causal factor
Elimination of selection bias
Improved control group recruitment
Reduced recall bias regarding pesticide use

correct_answer.text: Inadvertent matching for a putative causal factor

questions.explanation: The source warns that overzealous matching may inadvertently result in matching for putative causal factors as well. If occupational exposure history is related to pesticide exposure (the suspected causal factor), matching on it could reduce the exposure difference between cases and controls, obscuring the association. While matching can increase power (A), this specific match may reduce study validity.

questions.question_text: A clinician wishes to determine whether early intervention in prodromal psychosis prevents progression to first-episode psychosis. Which study design would best answer this question?

options.text: Case-control study comparing prodromal individuals with and without intervention history
Experimental RCT randomizing prodromal individuals to early intervention or standard care
Cross-sectional study measuring current prodromal symptoms
Ecological study of regional intervention programs
Case series documenting treated prodromal individuals

correct_answer.text: Experimental RCT randomizing prodromal individuals to early intervention or standard care

questions.explanation: Questions about the effect of an intervention are best answered by experimental RCTs where the intervention is randomly assigned. This design establishes causality regarding treatment efficacy. Case-control studies are retrospective, cross-sectional studies measure prevalence, ecological studies examine group-level patterns, and case series are descriptive without comparison groups.

questions.question_text: An analytical study is best characterized by which feature?

options.text: Description of disease characteristics in a single group
Comparative analysis of groups to measure association between variables
Experimental manipulation of a single risk factor
Prospective follow-up without comparison groups
Population-level data analysis without individual-level measures

correct_answer.text: Comparative analysis of groups to measure association between variables

questions.explanation: Analytical studies as involving comparative analysis of two groups to measure the association between variables of interest (e.g. a disease and a risk factor). Descriptive studies lack comparisons (A). Experimental studies involve manipulation (C). Options D and E describe other designs.

questions.question_text: When matching controls to cases in a case-control study, groupwise matching is used rather than pairwise matching primarily because:

options.text: It increases study power
It is less time-consuming
It eliminates recall bias
It ensures equal numbers of controls
It improves case definition

correct_answer.text: It is less time-consuming

questions.explanation: That matching can be done in groupwise or pairwise fashion, with the latter being more time-consuming. Pairwise matching involves matching each control to an individual case, whereas groupwise matching involves matching groups of controls to groups of cases, making it more efficient and time-efficient. ---

questions.question_text: Cross-sectional studies are best suited to answer which clinical inquiry?

options.text: What are the causes of this adverse outcome?
How common is this condition in a population?
What is the long-term prognosis in exposed individuals?
Does this new intervention reduce disease incidence?
What is the relative risk associated with this exposure?

correct_answer.text: How common is this condition in a population?

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies provide a snapshot at a single point in time and directly measure prevalence—answering How common is a condition? Option A requires case-control or cohort designs. Option C requires cohort studies (prognosis). Option D requires experimental designs (RCTs). Option E requires cohort studies for relative risk calculation.

questions.question_text: A researcher is studying the relationship between prenatal lead exposure and childhood IQ. Which evidence would most strongly support causality: a well-designed cohort study showing this association?

options.text: Equal prevalence of lead exposure in cases and controls
Temporality established with lead exposure measured before IQ testing
A very large sample size with high statistical power
Controls matched on parental education level
Measurement of lead levels using the most sensitive available test

correct_answer.text: Temporality established with lead exposure measured before IQ testing

questions.explanation: Temporal sequence (exposure before outcome) is essential for inferring causality, which cohort studies uniquely establish by design. While large sample size (C), careful measurement (E), and matching (D) improve study quality, they do not establish causality. Option A (equal exposure) would contradict an association.

questions.question_text: A researcher is designing a study to investigate whether a new antipsychotic medication reduces relapse rates compared to standard treatment. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Case report
Cohort study
Qualitative study
RCT
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: RCT

questions.explanation: RCTs are ideal for assessing causality and the effect of treatment by randomising subjects to experimental and control groups, minimizing bias and confounding. The source explicitly indicates RCTs are appropriate for therapy/harm questions. Cohort studies could work but are less robust; case reports, qualitative studies, and ecological studies are unsuitable for treatment efficacy questions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scenarios would make a cross-sectional study's findings potentially non-generalizable to the broader population?

options.text: The study measured exposure and outcome simultaneously
The sample is not representative of the population; volunteer bias is present
The study identified only associations and not causality
The study did not include a control group
The study had a large sample size

correct_answer.text: The sample is not representative of the population; volunteer bias is present

questions.explanation: That for cross-sectional studies, the sample must be representative of the population—affects generalisability otherwise. Volunteer bias from low response rates can lead to selection bias and non-representative samples, compromising external validity. The other options describe limitations inherent to the design rather than generalisability issues.

questions.question_text: Observational studies in which subjects are followed forward in time to see who develops disease or outcome are called:

options.text: Case-control studies
Cross-sectional studies
Cohort studies
Case reports
Ecological studies

correct_answer.text: Cohort studies

questions.explanation: Cohort studies are analytical observational studies in which exposed or at-risk subjects are followed forward in time (prospectively) to determine who develops the outcome. This prospective, forward-looking design is the defining characteristic. Case-control studies are retrospective; cross-sectional studies measure at one time point; case reports have no comparison group.

questions.question_text: In interpreting results from a case-control study of occupational exposures and psychotic disorders, why is odds ratio rather than relative risk calculated?

options.text: Odds ratios are more valid for retrospective data
Incidence cannot be measured in case-control studies
Controls are selected independently of exposure
Cases may be matched to controls
The study lacks a control group

correct_answer.text: Incidence cannot be measured in case-control studies

questions.explanation: Case-control studies cannot measure incidence directly because subjects are not followed prospectively from exposure to outcome. Therefore, only odds ratios can be calculated, not relative risk. This is a fundamental limitation of the case-control design's retrospective nature.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of trauma exposure and post-traumatic stress disorder, recall bias would be most problematic because:

options.text: Cases and controls are selected from different sources
The study is prospective rather than retrospective
Subjects with PTSD may differentially remember and report past trauma compared to controls
Control group selection is random
Multiple causes of PTSD are examined

correct_answer.text: Subjects with PTSD may differentially remember and report past trauma compared to controls

questions.explanation: Recall bias occurs when the accuracy or completeness of recalling past exposure differs between groups. Individuals with PTSD (cases) may have enhanced or distorted memories of traumatic events compared to controls without PTSD, systematically biasing exposure estimates. This is a well-documented vulnerability of case-control studies.

questions.question_text: An analytical study of bipolar disorder etiology compares 200 cases with childhood trauma history to 200 controls without bipolar disorder. If 150 cases report trauma but only 80 controls report trauma, this finding suggests what relationship?

options.text: No association between trauma and bipolar disorder
Trauma is protective against bipolar disorder
A positive association between trauma exposure and bipolar disorder
Confounding by demographic factors
The study has proven causation

correct_answer.text: A positive association between trauma exposure and bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: Higher proportion of exposed cases (150/200 = 75%) versus controls (80/200 = 40%) indicates positive association—the hypothesis is supported by greater exposure prevalence among cases. Option A is false. Option B reverses the direction. Option D requires additional evidence. Option E overstates case-control limitations.

questions.question_text: When designing a case-control study examining antecedent risk factors for childhood-onset bipolar disorder, strict diagnostic criteria for defining cases are essential because:

options.text: They determine the control group selection
They ensure the case group is homogeneous and validates that subjects truly have the condition
They reduce the need for matching
They eliminate confounding variables
They allow measurement of incidence

correct_answer.text: They ensure the case group is homogeneous and validates that subjects truly have the condition

questions.explanation: Evidence emphasizes that defining a case is crucial – strict diagnostic criteria and eligibility criteria must be followed. This ensures that all cases actually have the condition being studied and that the case group is homogeneous, preventing misclassification and reducing bias.

questions.question_text: A study examining rates of mental health service utilization across different ethnic populations reports that ethnic group X uses services at lower rates and hypothesizes this is due to cultural beliefs about mental illness. This reasoning most likely represents:

options.text: Valid causal inference from group-level data
Ecological fallacy
Proper cohort study analysis
Appropriate case-control methodology
Confounding bias

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy

questions.explanation: Drawing individual-level conclusions (person's cultural beliefs cause lower service use) from group-level observations (ethnic group's service utilization rates) represents ecological fallacy. Individuals within the ethnic group may have varying beliefs and service use patterns that differ from the group average.

questions.question_text: What is the primary disadvantage of case-control studies that prevents direct calculation of relative risk?

options.text: Selection bias in case recruitment
Inability to measure incidence directly
Excessive cost and time requirement
Difficulty in matching cases and controls
High rates of loss to follow-up

correct_answer.text: Inability to measure incidence directly

questions.explanation: Case-control studies cannot measure incidence because they do not follow populations forward in time—they begin with existing cases and controls. Therefore, only odds ratios can be calculated, not relative risk. While selection bias (A), matching difficulties (D), and lack of cost-effectiveness exist, they do not explain the mathematical inability to calculate relative risk. Option E (attrition) is actually an advantage of case-control studies.

questions.question_text: A clinician wants to determine the prevalence of depression in a community following a natural disaster. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Randomised controlled trial
Case-control study
Cross-sectional study
Cohort study
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional study

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are most appropriate for prevalence questions and when determining the value of screening or diagnostic tests. They identify patterns of disease prevalence at a point in time. Cohort and case-control studies are better for aetiology; RCTs are for treatment; ecological studies examine population-level differences. ---

questions.question_text: A longitudinal study following individuals with untreated depression over 10 years documents the natural course of illness including remission, relapse, and progression to bipolar disorder. Which research question is this design specifically suited to address?

options.text: What is the prevalence of depression?
How effective is antidepressant medication?
What is the natural course of untreated depression and what factors predict outcomes?
Are depression and bipolar disorder caused by the same biological factors?
What is the diagnostic accuracy of depression screening tools?

correct_answer.text: What is the natural course of untreated depression and what factors predict outcomes?

questions.explanation: Prospective longitudinal studies are specifically helpful for studying the natural course of illness by repeatedly observing the same population over prolonged periods. This design captures spontaneous illness trajectories, remission patterns, and prognostic factors without intervention, directly addressing questions about natural history.

questions.question_text: A researcher seeks to understand patients' subjective experiences of living with schizophrenia. According to the source, which study methodology is most appropriate?

options.text: Controlled trial
Case-control study
Qualitative study
Cohort study
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Qualitative study

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that qualitative studies are appropriate for exploring meaning or health experience. This methodology captures subjective patient perspectives that quantitative designs cannot adequately address. Other options measure frequencies, associations, or interventions rather than subjective meaning.

questions.question_text: In designing a case-control study of anesthetic complications during surgery, what makes defining the case population particularly critical?

options.text: To minimize the number of controls needed
To ensure only truly affected individuals are enrolled with standardized criteria
To eliminate all selection bias from the study
To allow investigators to mask exposure status
To reduce cost through stricter inclusion criteria

correct_answer.text: To ensure only truly affected individuals are enrolled with standardized criteria

questions.explanation: That defining cases is crucial with strict diagnostic criteria and eligibility criteria to ensure a homogeneous case group for valid comparison. While case definition may indirectly affect cost (E) or selection procedures, its primary function is ensuring case validity through standardized criteria. Options C and D are aspirational but not guaranteed outcomes.

questions.question_text: Which matching ratio in case-control studies maximizes statistical power without additional benefit?

options.text: 1:1 matching of cases to controls
2:1 matching of cases to controls
3:1 matching of cases to controls
4:1 matching of cases to controls
5:1 matching of cases to controls

correct_answer.text: 4:1 matching of cases to controls

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that up to a 4:1 ratio, increasing the number of controls increases study power, but no additional power gain occurs beyond this threshold. Ratios below 4:1 provide suboptimal power. A 5:1 ratio (E) provides no benefit but increases cost without added statistical gain.

questions.question_text: A qualitative study explores the subjective experiences and meanings of recovery in individuals with schizophrenia through in-depth interviews. This methodology is best suited to answer which clinical enquiry?

options.text: How common is recovery in schizophrenia?
What are the causes of non-recovery?
What is the 'meaning' or health 'experience' of recovery?
What are the effects of antipsychotic medication?
Does psychosocial intervention improve outcomes?

correct_answer.text: What is the 'meaning' or health 'experience' of recovery?

questions.explanation: The source explicitly identifies qualitative studies as the best design to examine 'meaning' or health 'experience' in clinical research. Quantitative designs address prevalence, causation, outcomes, and treatment effects; qualitative studies elucidate subjective experiences and meanings.

questions.question_text: A case-control study examining maternal alcohol consumption and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders begins recruitment by defining strict diagnostic criteria for cases. Why is this methodological step critical?

options.text: To prevent recall bias in case ascertainment
To ensure comparability with control group recruitment procedures
To standardize case definition and ensure homogeneous study population
To reduce selection bias in exposure measurement
To increase the odds ratio effect size

correct_answer.text: To standardize case definition and ensure homogeneous study population

questions.explanation: That defining a case is crucial—strict diagnostic criteria and eligibility criteria must be followed. This ensures a homogeneous case group and valid comparison with controls. While case definition may indirectly affect other factors, its primary function is standardization.

questions.question_text: In a prospective cohort study of antipsychotic medication initiation and metabolic side effects, subjects are assembled based on exposure status and followed forward to detect outcomes. This prospective design has which advantage over case-control design for this research question?

options.text: It is less expensive
It is less time-consuming
Incidence and relative risk can be directly measured
Recall bias is eliminated
Causation is proven

correct_answer.text: Incidence and relative risk can be directly measured

questions.explanation: Prospective cohort studies follow subjects from exposure forward to outcome, allowing direct measurement of incidence rates and calculation of relative risk. Case-control studies, being retrospective, cannot measure incidence and provide only odds ratios. This is a fundamental advantage of prospective designs.

questions.question_text: A case-control study recruits 100 cases of major depression and 400 controls to investigate genetic and environmental risk factors. Which statement best explains the efficiency of this 4:1 ratio?

options.text: It maximizes statistical power without further efficiency gains from additional controls
It reduces the number of variables that can be examined
It requires smaller effect sizes to achieve significance
It eliminates the need for matching
It prevents selection bias

correct_answer.text: It maximizes statistical power without further efficiency gains from additional controls

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that up to a 4:1 ratio, increasing controls increases power, but power does not increase beyond this ratio. Therefore, 4:1 represents the optimal efficient ratio—adding more controls would not provide additional benefits.

questions.question_text: A researcher measures current depressive symptoms and family history of depression simultaneously in a primary care population. Which study design is being employed, and what is its primary limitation regarding causality?

options.text: Cohort study; cannot establish incidence
Case-control study; temporality is unclear
Cross-sectional study; exposure and outcome are measured together, making causal direction uncertain
Longitudinal study; is too time-consuming
Experimental study; requires randomization

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional study; exposure and outcome are measured together, making causal direction uncertain

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome together at a single point in time, creating temporal ambiguity about which variable preceded the other. This makes establishing causal direction difficult. While cross-sectional studies can suggest putative relationships, they are not ideal for determining causality.

questions.question_text: In a cross-sectional study examining the prevalence of anxiety in university students, the response rate is only 15%. What is the main threat to the validity of this study?

options.text: Loss to follow-up
Recall bias
Volunteer bias—low response rates suggest the sample may not be representative
Publication bias
Selection from control group

correct_answer.text: Volunteer bias—low response rates suggest the sample may not be representative

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are specifically vulnerable to volunteer bias because response rates can be very low, and the sample must be representative of the population. A 15% response rate raises serious concerns about whether respondents differ systematically from non-respondents, affecting generalisability. Loss to follow-up is irrelevant to cross-sectional studies; recall bias is less salient than volunteer bias here. ---

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of clinical audit?

options.text: To establish causality between an exposure and outcome
To measure current performance against established standards or criteria
To generate novel hypotheses about disease mechanisms
To randomly assign patients to treatment groups
To provide prevalence data for a population

correct_answer.text: To measure current performance against established standards or criteria

questions.explanation: Clinical audit measures current performance against established standards/criteria. However, a limitation is that meeting criteria doesn't indicate how well things were done—it provides an unreliable estimate of effectiveness. Audit is not designed to establish causality (experimental studies do this) or generate hypotheses (descriptive studies do this). ---

questions.question_text: A case-control study examining the association between sedentary lifestyle and depression includes matching for age, sex, and employment status. Which scenario would represent problematic overzealous matching?

options.text: Matching for age (a demographic confounder)
Matching for employment status (a socioeconomic indicator)
Matching for physical activity level itself (a putative causal factor)
Matching for sex (a demographic variable)
Matching for residence location (to control for regional variation)

correct_answer.text: Matching for physical activity level itself (a putative causal factor)

questions.explanation: Matching on putative causal factors or intermediate variables can inadvertently mask the association being investigated by making the exposed and unexposed groups too similar on the exposure pathway. The source warns that overzealous matching may inadvertently result in matching for putative causal factors as well, obscuring true associations.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of oral contraceptive use and venous thromboembolism, controls are recruited from patients presenting with peptic ulcer disease. Which potential problem does this introduce?

options.text: Overmatching for a causal factor
Selection bias in the control group
Recall bias regarding medication use
Confounding by indication
Ecological fallacy in interpretation

correct_answer.text: Selection bias in the control group

questions.explanation: Hospital-based controls with a different disease may not be representative of the source population from which cases arose, introducing selection bias. While peptic ulcer disease itself may not be related to oral contraceptive use, using hospitalized patients with any condition as controls can distort exposure prevalence estimates. Overmatching (A) refers to matching on variables associated with exposure. Recall bias (C) and confounding (D) are general biases but not specific to this control selection. Ecological fallacy (E) applies only to ecological studies.

questions.question_text: Longitudinal studies are particularly valuable for identifying which epidemiological measure?

options.text: Point prevalence of disease in a community
Incidence rates of disease in a cohort
Proportion of exposed individuals in the general population
Odds ratio of exposure among cases
Ecological associations between population-level variables

correct_answer.text: Incidence rates of disease in a cohort

questions.explanation: That prospective longitudinal studies are helpful for finding incidence rates by observing disease onset over time in the same population. Point prevalence (A) is measured in cross-sectional studies. Options C, D, and E represent outcomes better addressed by other designs.

questions.question_text: Which study design is most appropriate for evaluating the effectiveness of a novel antipsychotic in routine clinical practice?

options.text: Experimental RCT
Pragmatic RCT
Uncontrolled trial
Ecological study
Case series

correct_answer.text: Pragmatic RCT

questions.explanation: Evidence indicates, pragmatic RCTs (systematic reviews) are the best design to answer treatment effectiveness questions in real-world conditions. Experimental RCTs (A) evaluate efficacy under controlled conditions, not effectiveness in practice. Uncontrolled trials (C) lack comparison groups. Ecological studies (D) and case series (E) cannot establish causality.

questions.question_text: In a cohort study examining the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, which temporal relationship is demonstrated?

options.text: Exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously
Exposure is assessed before the outcome occurs
Outcome is identified before exposure is documented
Both exposure and outcome are identified from historical records
The study begins with population-level aggregate data

correct_answer.text: Exposure is assessed before the outcome occurs

questions.explanation: Cohort studies are prospective by design—researchers identify exposed individuals and follow them forward in time to observe whether outcomes develop. This establishes the required temporal relationship for causality. Options A and E describe cross-sectional and ecological designs respectively. Options C and D describe retrospective case-control designs.

questions.question_text: Evidence-based medicine is defined as the conscientious use of current best evidence integrated with which two additional components?

options.text: Clinical expertise and patient values
Clinical expertise and historical precedent
Patient values and institutional guidelines
Institutional guidelines and expert opinion
Historical precedent and institutional consensus

correct_answer.text: Clinical expertise and patient values

questions.explanation: EBM requires integration of three components: individual clinical expertise, best available external clinical evidence from systematic research, and the patient's unique values and circumstances. Options B, C, D, and E omit or misrepresent one of these core elements; expertise paired with historical precedent (rather than current evidence) is not EBM.

questions.question_text: A 10-year cohort study of depression treatment outcomes finds that patients treated with psychotherapy alone have lower relapse rates than untreated controls. Which interpretation is most valid?

options.text: Psychotherapy causes prevention of relapse
Psychotherapy is more effective than medication
There is an association between psychotherapy and lower relapse rates
Untreated depression inevitably leads to relapse
Psychotherapy should replace all psychiatric medications

correct_answer.text: There is an association between psychotherapy and lower relapse rates

questions.explanation: Cohort studies establish temporal relationships and associations but cannot definitively prove causality because of potential confounding—treated patients may differ from untreated controls in motivation, severity, or other factors. Option A overstates causality. Options B, D, and E make unsupported claims beyond what the design can demonstrate.

questions.question_text: A survey administered to all psychiatric outpatients in a health system measures current symptom burden, functional impairment, and service satisfaction. This descriptive study design is best suited to answer which question?

options.text: Do psychosocial interventions reduce symptom burden?
What are the characteristics and attributes of this patient population?
What causes persistent symptoms?
Does early intervention prevent disease progression?
What is the prognostic significance of specific symptoms?

correct_answer.text: What are the characteristics and attributes of this patient population?

questions.explanation: Descriptive studies describe the characteristics present in members of a study group and discuss the distribution of these characteristics. They do not test causal hypotheses or make comparisons with other groups. This survey design captures attributes of the existing patient population without comparison groups or interventions.

questions.question_text: An epidemiologist observes that countries with low religious attachment have high suicide rates and concludes that low religiosity causes suicide. Which logical fallacy has occurred?

options.text: Confounding bias
Ecological fallacy
Selection bias
Recall bias
Reverse causality

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy

questions.explanation: The source directly illustrates ecological fallacy using this exact example—drawing individual-level conclusions from group-level data. The individuals who commit suicide in low-religiosity countries may or may not be religious themselves. This is not confounding (A), selection (C), or recall bias (D), and the temporal direction is not reversed (E).

questions.question_text: In a prospective cohort study of psychosocial risk factors for depression, which statement regarding study power is accurate?

options.text: Larger samples always provide greater power regardless of follow-up duration
Long-term follow-up with substantial attrition enhances statistical power
Study design and sample size interact to determine power
Power is determined solely by statistical significance
Cohort studies have inherently greater power than case-control studies

correct_answer.text: Study design and sample size interact to determine power

questions.explanation: Study power depends on multiple factors including sample size, effect size, significance level, and for cohort studies, follow-up duration and attrition rates. While larger samples generally increase power, this interaction is not absolute—loss to follow-up, effect sizes, and other design features critically influence power.

questions.question_text: Which feature distinguishes a census from a typical survey?

options.text: Census measures different variables
Census uses qualitative methodology
Census includes the entire population as its sample
Census cannot estimate prevalence
Census is conducted prospectively

correct_answer.text: Census includes the entire population as its sample

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines census as a special cross-sectional study where instead of a subset, the sample includes the whole of the population. All other characteristics remain identical to surveys. This distinction is fundamental and explicit in the source.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a strength of ecological studies?

options.text: They establish individual-level causality
They are cheaper to conduct and rely on previously collected data
They eliminate confounding variables
They require prospective follow-up
They are immune to selection bias

correct_answer.text: They are cheaper to conduct and rely on previously collected data

questions.explanation: The source lists strengths of ecological studies as being cheaper to conduct, as they rely on data previously collected and being easier to obtain data at the population level. A major limitation is ecological fallacy—not a strength; they do not establish causality, require follow-up, or eliminate bias.

questions.question_text: A hospital-based case-control study of medication side effects recruits cases from an inpatient psychiatric ward and controls from the same hospital's outpatient clinic. Which potential bias is introduced by this selection strategy?

options.text: Information bias
Selection bias—controls may have different hospitalization risk than cases
Confounding by disease severity
Attrition bias
Detection bias

correct_answer.text: Selection bias—controls may have different hospitalization risk than cases

questions.explanation: Using hospital-based controls introduces selection bias if controls have systematically different characteristics than the source population from which cases arose. Hospitalized cases may differ fundamentally from outpatient controls in disease severity, medication exposure, and comorbidity, making the groups non-comparable on dimensions beyond exposure status.

questions.question_text: In a cohort study, what must be true about exposure status at the study's inception?

options.text: Exposure status must be equal in all participants
Exposure status must be assessed before outcome measurement
Exposure status must be randomly assigned to participants
Exposure status must be unknown to the researcher
Exposure status must be identical to the control group

correct_answer.text: Exposure status must be assessed before outcome measurement

questions.explanation: Cohort studies require that exposure is documented before outcome occurs, establishing temporality essential for causality assessment. Option A violates the definition of a cohort (heterogeneous exposure). Option C describes experimental design. Option D contradicts the observational nature. Option E contradicts the comparative design.

questions.question_text: In descriptive studies, what is the primary purpose regarding hypothesis testing?

options.text: To develop and test causal hypotheses
To compare characteristics across multiple groups
To describe characteristics and distribution in a study group
To establish cause-and-effect relationships
To measure odds ratios and relative risks

correct_answer.text: To describe characteristics and distribution in a study group

questions.explanation: That descriptive studies aim to describe the characteristics of a group of subjects and There is no testing of a causal hypothesis or any comparisons with other groups. Descriptive studies characterize populations; analytical studies test hypotheses (A, B, D, E).

questions.question_text: Which study design is most appropriate for testing the efficacy of a new antipsychotic medication in first-episode psychosis?

options.text: Case control study
Cross-sectional study
Randomised controlled trial
Ecological study
Case report

correct_answer.text: Randomised controlled trial

questions.explanation: RCTs are the gold standard for assessing therapy and treatment efficacy, as they can minimise bias and confounding through experimental design with control groups. Case control and cross-sectional studies are observational and unsuitable for causal inference about treatment. Ecological studies and case reports cannot adequately test efficacy. ---

questions.question_text: Which characteristic distinguishes experimental studies from observational studies?

options.text: Experimental studies are always cheaper
Experimental studies involve researcher assignment of exposure; observational studies do not
Observational studies are always higher quality
Experimental studies cannot measure outcomes
Observational studies always establish causality

correct_answer.text: Experimental studies involve researcher assignment of exposure; observational studies do not

questions.explanation: Experimental studies (e.g., RCTs) involve researcher assignment of subjects to experimental or control groups to minimize bias and confounding. Observational studies (descriptive or analytical) do not involve researcher assignment of exposure; participants' exposures are observed naturally. This is the defining distinction.

questions.question_text: An ecological study finds that regions with higher rates of mental health service utilisation have lower suicide rates. Which caution is essential when interpreting this finding?

options.text: The study lacks statistical power
The finding is necessarily invalid
Ecological fallacy—the region-level correlation does not mean individuals who use services are those with lower suicide rates
Publication bias has distorted the results
Confounding variables cannot exist in ecological studies

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy—the region-level correlation does not mean individuals who use services are those with lower suicide rates

questions.explanation: Ecological fallacy is the key limitation—population-level associations do not equate to individual-level biological effects. High service utilisation at the regional level may involve different individuals than those at risk for suicide. This is a fundamental interpretive error specific to ecological studies. The finding may be valid, but individual-level inferences cannot be made. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher conducts a cross-sectional survey assessing depression prevalence in healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Which bias is the study design MOST vulnerable to in this context?

options.text: Recall bias
Selection bias from low response rates (volunteer bias)
Loss to follow-up bias
Channelling bias
Detection bias

correct_answer.text: Selection bias from low response rates (volunteer bias)

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional surveys are specifically vulnerable to volunteer bias due to low response rates and the requirement for a representative sample. Healthcare workers with higher stress/depression may be more likely to participate than well workers (or vice versa), creating non-representative sampling. Loss to follow-up is irrelevant to cross-sectional design; recall bias is minimal for current depression. ---

questions.question_text: A case-control study recruiting cases from hospital diabetic clinics and controls from the general population hospital waiting room could face which problem in interpreting results?

options.text: Loss to follow-up
Temporal ambiguity regarding exposure onset
Unequal selection procedures between cases and controls
Inability to measure odds ratios
Reverse causality

correct_answer.text: Unequal selection procedures between cases and controls

questions.explanation: Evidence emphasizes that controls must be recruited independently of exposure status and come from a comparable source population. Using different recruitment settings (diabetic clinics vs. waiting rooms) violates this principle. This is selection bias due to unequal recruitment procedures. Options A, B, and E are not case-control limitations. Option D is false.

questions.question_text: Which study design is most appropriate for investigating a suspected causative association between a risk factor and a rare disease?

options.text: Case-control study
Case report
Cohort study
Cross-sectional study
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Case-control study

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are explicitly suited for investigating rare diseases because they start with cases (diseased subjects) and work backwards to exposure, making them efficient when disease prevalence is low. Cohort studies would be inefficient for rare diseases as they require following large populations prospectively. Case reports lack comparative groups. Cross-sectional and ecological studies cannot establish causality or temporality.

questions.question_text: Why are relatives of patients particularly useful as controls in case-control studies of genetic psychiatric disorders?

options.text: They are always willing to participate
They share genetic and environmental backgrounds while remaining free of disease
They eliminate the possibility of selection bias
They allow direct calculation of heritability
They increase the odds ratio magnitude

correct_answer.text: They share genetic and environmental backgrounds while remaining free of disease

questions.explanation: Relatives as controls provide genetic similarity and often shared environmental factors while remaining unaffected, creating good comparability to cases while maintaining exposure independence. This is a strategic control selection method. Options A and C are unsupported, and options D and E misstate the design purpose.

questions.question_text: In a retrospective case-control study of antipsychotic medication adherence and psychotic relapse, recall bias is particularly problematic for which variable?

options.text: The diagnosis of schizophrenia at study entry
The hospitalization record for psychotic relapse
Patients' reports of medication adherence over the past year
Age and gender of participants
The psychiatric facility where treatment occurred

correct_answer.text: Patients' reports of medication adherence over the past year

questions.explanation: Recall bias most affects subjective historical data requiring memory over extended periods—medication adherence over a year requires participants to accurately recall past behavior. Objective outcomes like hospitalization (B) are less prone to recall bias. Demographic variables (D, E) and clear diagnoses (A) are factual and less affected by memory limitations.

questions.question_text: A clinician wishes to evaluate a new diagnostic test for detecting depression against the established diagnostic criteria. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Case-control study
Cohort study
Cross-sectional comparison to gold standard
Ecological study
Case series

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional comparison to gold standard

questions.explanation: That cross-sectional comparison to a gold standard is the appropriate design for diagnostic assessment. This design measures sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values by comparing the new test against the established diagnostic standard simultaneously. Case-control (A) and cohort (B) designs do not address diagnostic accuracy.

questions.question_text: Why are longitudinal studies more costly and time-consuming than cross-sectional studies?

options.text: They require more outcome assessment procedures
Researchers must follow participants repeatedly over extended periods
Statistical analysis is more complex
Multiple control groups must be maintained
Baseline assessment of exposure requires greater precision

correct_answer.text: Researchers must follow participants repeatedly over extended periods

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states longitudinal studies are costly and time consuming because observations must be repeated in the same population over a prolonged time, requiring extended follow-up contact and repeated measurement. While other factors may contribute, the fundamental reason is the repeated assessment requirement over time.

questions.question_text: A descriptive study documents psychiatric symptoms, substance use, and social functioning in a sample of 50 individuals experiencing homelessness. The key characteristic distinguishing this from an analytical study is:

options.text: The study is cross-sectional rather than longitudinal
There is no comparison with other groups or testing of causal hypotheses
The sample size is small
No outcome measure is used
Subjects are not exposed to any risks

correct_answer.text: There is no comparison with other groups or testing of causal hypotheses

questions.explanation: Descriptive studies describe characteristics of a study group without testing causal hypotheses or comparing with other groups. Analytical studies involve comparative analysis of two groups to measure associations. The distinction is fundamental and applies regardless of study size, temporal design, or sample characteristics.

questions.question_text: A case-control study examines risk factors for schizophrenia in individuals exposed to childhood trauma. Which type of evidence question is this study design best suited to answer?

options.text: Prognosis
Therapy/treatment efficacy
Aetiology
Diagnosis
Harm from intervention

correct_answer.text: Aetiology

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are specifically suitable for aetiology questions. They start with cases (those with schizophrenia) and controls (those without) and look backward to assess exposure to risk factors (childhood trauma). This allows assessment of associations between exposures and disease development. ---

questions.question_text: In comparing case-control and cohort studies for investigating aetiology, which advantage does a cohort study have over a case-control study?

options.text: Lower cost
Faster to complete
Can directly establish temporal relationships between exposure and outcome
Easier to recruit participants
Better for rare diseases

correct_answer.text: Can directly establish temporal relationships between exposure and outcome

questions.explanation: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time, directly establishing that exposure precedes outcome (temporal relationship). Case-control studies are retrospective and infer temporal relationships. Both are suitable for aetiology, but cohort studies provide stronger temporal evidence. Cohort studies are more expensive, time-consuming, and problematic for rare diseases. ---
